name: Nutrition & Dietetics
hook: Counseling practice at volume, plus a teaching tool students can hand to an actual community group.

make.body: Portion and plate-method models that students design for a specific community they are working with, in the foods that community actually eats. Generic food models exist commercially; models built around local staples do not, and making that argument is half the assignment.

build.body: A standardized client for motivational interviewing practice: someone with a real cultural food context, a budget constraint, and a reason to resist. Students run the session repeatedly, which is impossible with human volunteers.

plan.txt: Students select a community partner and a specific counseling scenario. Draft the client profile they will need.
Build the AI client and run three sessions, submitting transcripts. Grade whether the student did more listening than telling.
Design and submit the physical teaching model. Requirement: justify every food choice against the partner community.
Field test the model with the partner and revise once based on what confused people.

prompt: Role-play as a nutrition counseling client for a dietetics student. You are [age, situation, cultural food background, budget constraint]. You are here because someone else told you to come, and you are polite but not really convinced you need to change anything. Do not volunteer information unless I ask a good question. Do not become enthusiastic and cooperative just because I say something encouraging. Stay in character until I type END SESSION, then give me feedback on whether I actually listened.
tryTuesday: 90 minutes, no fabrication. Minutes 0–15: students draft a one-paragraph client profile grounded in a specific local community and food context — a Waipahu household, a kūpuna center. Minutes 15–70: each student runs the standardized-client prompt and conducts a motivational-interviewing session, recording a talk-time tally of how many minutes they spent asking versus telling. Minutes 70–90: pairs review each other's transcripts and mark the first place the student slipped into advice-giving before the client felt heard. The graded artifact is the transcript plus the talk-time tally; it measures whether the student listened more than they instructed.

replaces.assignment: The written diet-plan case study submitted for a hypothetical patient.
replaces.lost: The detailed nutrient-calculation and meal-planning documentation.
replaces.gained: Students practice the counseling relationship — the part that determines whether any plan is followed — at a volume human standardized patients cannot provide, and they are graded on listening rather than on a plan the patient never agreed to.

aiFailsHere: A model asked for nutrition guidance defaults to generic, culturally flat advice — 'reduce portion sizes, choose whole grains' — that ignores budget, access, and the foods a specific community actually eats, delivered with a confidence that erases the patient's autonomy. Playing a client, it also tends to reward the counselor, opening up as soon as the student says something kind, teaching exactly the wrong reflex unless the prompt forbids it.

rubric.description: The session shows more eliciting than instructing; the talk-time tally and open-question count bear this out.
Recommendations engage the client's actual foods, budget, and household rather than generic guidance.
Uses reflections and affirmations that demonstrate the client was heard before change is discussed.
Supports the client's own reasons for change instead of prescribing; does not accept the AI's premature cooperation as success.

budget.perStudentCost: $0 for the Tuesday version; roughly $4–8 per student in filament for portion and plate-method models in the four-week build.
budget.fileDueWeek: Week 3 — print file due end of week 3 so models return for the week-4 field test.
budget.calendarNote: Counseling reps need no lead time; the teaching models depend on the 7–10 day print turnaround.

scales.oneSession: The 90-minute standardized-client session with a talk-time tally; no fabrication.
scales.fourWeeks: The seeded four-week plan: draft the client profile, run and submit intake transcripts, design and submit the teaching model, then field-test and revise with the partner community.
scales.oneSemester: A full community-partner project — repeated counseling reps, a printed teaching model built around local staples, a field test with the partner community, and one documented revision based on what confused people.

promptOutput.model: Claude (Anthropic) — captured 2026-07-27 in an isolated fresh session with no build context; output is unedited.
promptOutput.promptFilled: Filled in as a 58-year-old Filipino grandfather in Waipahu, newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes, on a fixed income, cooking rice-and-pork dishes for a household of six, attending because his daughter told him to.
promptOutput.output:
Good morning. Oh, I'm okay, I'm okay. Cannot complain.

My daughter, she made the appointment for me. She's the one always worrying. So I told her okay, I come, I sit, I listen. You know how they are.

I feel fine, though. No pain, nothing. Still going every day.

annotations.marker: Stayed guarded and minimal: 'I'm okay, I'm okay. Cannot complain.'
annotations.note: The model correctly withheld information and did not volunteer, giving the student something to actually elicit — faithful standardized-client behavior.

annotations.marker: Externalized motivation: 'My daughter... made the appointment'
annotations.note: Accurately models pre-contemplation; the student must build rapport before the client engages, which is the point of the exercise.

annotations.marker: Register choices ('You know how they are')
annotations.note: A plausible cultural-register performance, but a place for care — the student should attend to the real person, not a caricature the model sketches.

annotations.marker: Ends the turn open, not cooperative
annotations.note: It did not reward a mere greeting with disclosure, exactly the trap the prompt was written to avoid.

related.reason: Both run a standardized-client intake graded on whether the student listened and earned disclosure rather than dispensing advice.
Both require designing a physical teaching object for a specific real community or classroom and justifying every choice against that audience.
